processes.name: Judicial review
processes.plainName: Asking a court to check the decision was made lawfully
processes.oneLine: A court checks whether the decision was made the right way — not whether it was a good decision.
processes.question: Was the decision made lawfully?
processes.whatItIs: Judicial review is different from merits review. A court does not ask whether the decision was right or fair — it asks whether it was made lawfully: did the decision-maker have the power, follow a fair process, and stay within the law? If the court finds a legal error — a 'ground of review' — it can set the decision aside. But the court cannot make a new decision for you. It usually sends the matter back to be decided again, properly.

bodies.name: The Federal Court / Federal Circuit and Family Court
bodies.note: judicial review of Australian Government decisions (ADJR Act; s 39B Judiciary Act).

bodies.name: The High Court
bodies.note: constitutional judicial review of Commonwealth officers (s 75(v) Constitution).

bodies.name: The Supreme Court of Victoria
bodies.note: the Victorian equivalent, for state government decisions. There are two ways in, and they have different time limits, so this is worth asking a free legal service about early.

canApply: You need a 'ground of review' — a specific legal error in how the decision was made.
You usually need to be a person affected by the decision (standing).
There are strict time limits, and they are usually NOT paused by asking for reasons.
whatHappens: You start a proceeding in the court.
You argue that one or more grounds of review apply.
The court looks at the legality of the decision, not its merits.
If a ground is made out, the court can set the decision aside.
remedies: Send it back (remit) to be decided again, lawfully.
Orders to require or stop action, in some cases.
A declaration — a formal statement of what the legal position is, without ordering anyone to do anything.
limits: The court cannot substitute its own decision — it cannot simply give you the outcome you want, only require a lawful re-decision.
Judicial review is about legality, not about whether the decision was harsh or wrong on the facts.
goodToKnow: A refusal counts as a decision. Being told no is something you can ask about.
A failure to decide can count too, where they had a duty to decide and did not.
A tribunal's own decision can be judicially reviewed. The tribunal acts under a law too, so a court can check that it kept within the law.
A court will not simply disagree with the result. It looks at whether the decision was made lawfully.
Judicial review can be technical and the time limits are tight — getting free legal help early really matters.

processes.name: Merits review
processes.plainName: Asking for a fresh look at the decision
processes.oneLine: A tribunal looks at your case again and can make a different decision.
processes.question: Is this the correct or preferable decision?
processes.whatItIs: Merits review means an independent tribunal looks at the decision again — on the facts and the law — as if it were being made fresh. The tribunal stands in the shoes of the original decision-maker. It must apply the same rules that bound them, so it is not free to decide on general fairness alone. It can agree with the decision, change part of it, or replace it with a different one. It is usually cheaper, faster, and less formal than going to court.

bodies.name: The Administrative Review Tribunal (ART)
bodies.note: hears many Australian Government decisions, such as Centrelink.

bodies.name: VCAT (the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal)
bodies.note: the Victorian equivalent, for state decisions where an Act gives a right of review.

canApply: There must be a law that gives a right of review for this kind of decision.
You usually need to be a person affected by the decision (this is called standing).
There is almost always a time limit — this is the part people miss most.
If the time limit has passed, the tribunal can still be asked to allow a late application. It does not have to say yes, but it can be asked.
whatHappens: You lodge an application with the tribunal.
Often there is an informal stage that tries to sort it out first.
If it goes to a hearing, you explain your side and give your evidence.
The tribunal makes a fresh decision.
remedies: Affirm — keep the decision the same.
Vary — change part of the decision.
Set aside and substitute — replace it with a new decision.
Remit — send it back to the original decision-maker to be made again, with directions about how.
limits: Merits review is only available where a law provides it — not every decision can be reviewed on the merits.
A tribunal is not a court. It sits inside government, and it is doing administration rather than deciding a legal dispute between you and the state.
Government policy can guide the tribunal, but it cannot decide the matter for it.
goodToKnow: Because the tribunal can change the outcome, merits review is usually what people want when they disagree with the result.
The tribunal decides on the best and most current information. So you can usually give it things that did not exist when the first decision was made, such as a new medical report.
The tribunal applies the same rules the first decision-maker had to apply. It is not free to decide on general fairness alone.

comparison.intro: Most decisions can be challenged in one of two ways. They ask different questions, so the right one depends on what you are hoping for.

rows.mr: Is this the correct or preferable decision?

rows.jr: A court (Supreme Court or Federal Court)

rows.mr: The facts and the law, fresh
rows.jr: Only how the decision was made — its legality
Set it aside and send it back — not replace it

rows.mr: The best and most current evidence. You can give them new information.
rows.jr: Usually only what was in front of the original decision-maker.

rows.mr: Whoever the law for that decision says can apply
rows.jr: A person with a real interest in the decision
More formal, and often needs a lawyer

rows.mr: Usually free, or a low fee
rows.jr: Court fees. You may also be ordered to pay the other side's costs.

rows.mr: Only where a law gives a review right for that decision
rows.jr: Generally available. Whether there was a legal error is the question a court decides, not a condition for asking. A law cannot take that power away from the court.

options.prompt: A different outcome — I think the decision is wrong
options.because: If you want the decision changed, merits review (where it is available) is usually the path, because a tribunal can replace the decision.

options.prompt: The decision was made unfairly or without power
options.because: If the problem is how the decision was made, judicial review asks a court to check that it was lawful.

options.prompt: Both might apply, or I am not sure
options.because: Sometimes both are possible, and the time limits are different. A free legal service can help you choose — and quickly, because of the time limits.

faq.q: What is the difference between merits review and judicial review?
faq.a: Merits review asks whether the decision is the correct or preferable one — a tribunal looks at it again and can change or replace it. Judicial review asks whether the decision was made lawfully — a court checks how it was made and can set it aside, but cannot make a new decision for you.

If you want a different outcome, merits review (where a law provides it) is usually the path. If the problem is how the decision was made, judicial review checks its legality. The time limits are different, so a free legal service can help you choose quickly.

faq.q: Can I use both merits review and judicial review?
faq.a: Sometimes both are possible. They have different time limits, so it is worth getting free legal advice early so you do not miss one.

faq.q: If both are open, which one comes first?
faq.a: Where a law gives a right to merits review, that is usually the step people take first. It costs less, it can change the outcome, and a fresh decision may settle the matter without a court. Judicial review does not disappear in the meantime — it stays open for the legality questions.

faq.q: What if the tribunal decides against me too?
faq.a: A tribunal's decision is itself a decision made under a law. That means it can be judicially reviewed as well, on the same legality grounds — for example if the tribunal applied the wrong test or did not give you a fair hearing. This is technical, so it is worth free legal help.

faq.q: Is there one first step that helps either way?
faq.a: Asking for the reasons in writing helps with both. It is usually free, and it shows you what the decision-maker actually relied on. That is what tells you whether your complaint is about the outcome or about how the decision was made.

faq.q: Can I give them new information?
faq.a: At merits review, usually yes. The tribunal decides on the best and most current evidence, so it can look at things that did not exist when the first decision was made. Judicial review is different — a court usually looks only at what was in front of the original decision-maker.

faq.q: Could I have to pay the government's legal costs?
faq.a: At a tribunal, usually not — merits review is designed to be low-cost and people often act for themselves. Judicial review is a court case, so there are court fees and a court can order you to pay the other side's costs. This is one reason to get free legal help before filing in a court.

faq.q: Is merits review or judicial review cheaper?
faq.a: Merits review at a tribunal is usually cheaper and less formal than going to court for judicial review. Many tribunal reviews are free or low-cost; check the rule for your decision.

grounds.name: Bad faith
grounds.plainName: The decision was not made honestly
grounds.oneLine: The decision was made dishonestly, or for a deliberately improper reason.
grounds.whatItMeans: A decision made dishonestly, or for a deliberately improper reason, can be unlawful. Bad faith is rare and hard to prove, and it is a serious allegation — it means much more than a mistake or even an unfair process.
grounds.plainExample: A decision is made to deliberately harm someone for personal reasons.
whatRelates: There are real signs the decision was not made honestly.
The decision looks deliberately aimed at harming you for an improper reason.
grounds.whatItIsNot: It does not cover an honest mistake or an unfair process — those are other grounds. Bad faith is a high bar and a serious claim.
grounds.test: A decision made in bad faith may be invalid; it is a serious allegation that needs strong material.

elements.name: Dishonesty or deliberate impropriety
elements.layPrompt: Are there real signs the decision was not made honestly?

leadingCases.name: SBBS v Minister for Immigration and Multicultural and Indigenous Affairs (2002) 194 ALR 749
leadingCases.explains: What bad faith requires — a serious allegation of dishonesty that is rarely made out.

grounds.name: Consequences of a breach
grounds.plainName: Does breaking the rule make the decision invalid?
grounds.oneLine: Not every mistake makes a decision invalid.
grounds.whatItMeans: Sometimes a rule was not followed. The next question is what that means. Some mistakes make a decision invalid. Others do not. It depends on what the Act intended, and on whether the mistake could have changed the outcome.
grounds.plainExample: An office missed a step it was meant to follow. Whether that undoes the decision depends on the Act.
whatRelates: A step in the process was skipped.
You were not given something the rules say you get.
A time frame in the rules was not kept to.
Something went wrong that might have changed the answer.
grounds.whatItIsNot: This is not a ground on its own. It is the question that follows once something has gone wrong. It is also not a single rule for every mistake: a few problems are serious enough to count without asking whether they changed the outcome.
grounds.test: Whether a mistake makes a decision invalid depends on the purpose of the Act, and on whether the mistake could have made a difference. Some problems do not need that second step. Bias and unreasonableness count on their own.

elements.name: The step that was missed
elements.layPrompt: Was there a step in the process that did not happen?

elements.name: Whether it could have mattered
elements.layPrompt: Could that have changed what was decided?

leadingCases.name: Project Blue Sky Inc v Australian Broadcasting Authority (1998) 194 CLR 355
leadingCases.explains: Whether breaking a rule makes an act invalid depends on what the Act intended.

leadingCases.name: LPDT v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs (2024) 280 CLR 321
leadingCases.explains: Some mistakes are serious enough that the decision loses the character the law requires.

leadingCases.name: Hossain v Minister for Immigration and Border Protection (2018) 264 CLR 123
leadingCases.explains: A mistake usually has to be able to change the outcome to matter.

leadingCases.name: Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs v Bhardwaj (2002) 209 CLR 597
leadingCases.explains: Where the error goes to the power itself, the law treats what happened as no decision at all.

grounds.name: Human rights were not properly considered (Victoria)
grounds.plainName: They did not properly think about your human rights
grounds.oneLine: In Victoria, a public authority has to give real thought to your human rights.
grounds.whatItMeans: Victoria has a Charter of human rights. It binds public authorities in Victoria. It asks two things of them. They must not act in a way that is not compatible with your human rights. They must also give proper consideration to any human right the decision affects. Proper consideration means real thought, not a box ticked.
grounds.plainExample: A public body decides where you will live. Nothing in the reasons shows anyone thought about what that would mean for your family.
whatRelates: A Victorian public authority made the decision.
The decision affects something personal — your home, your family, your privacy, or how you were treated.
The reasons never mention your rights at all.
The reasons mention your rights, but only as a heading.
A right was limited, and the reasons do not explain why that was needed.
grounds.whatItIsNot: This is not a case you win on its own. Breaking this duty is unlawful, but by itself it does not automatically make the decision invalid. It usually runs alongside another ground rather than replacing one. It also applies only in Victoria.
grounds.test: A public authority must not act incompatibly with a human right, and must give proper consideration to a relevant human right. Proper consideration is a higher standard than the ordinary duty to take a relevant matter into account.

elements.name: A Victorian public authority
elements.layPrompt: Was the decision made by a Victorian public body?

elements.name: A human right the decision touches
elements.layPrompt: Did the decision affect something the Charter protects, such as your home, your family, or your privacy?

elements.name: Real thought about the effect on you
elements.layPrompt: Do the reasons show they thought about what this would mean for you?

elements.name: Whether limiting the right was justified
elements.layPrompt: If a right was limited, do the reasons explain why that limit was necessary?

sources: Owner's administrative-law knowledge base (Combined MR/JR Framework; JR Hypo, 2026-08-19)

leadingCases.name: Bare v IBAC
leadingCases.explains: Proper consideration has two sides. One is about the thinking. It asks whether they really turned their mind to the effect on you.

leadingCases.name: Certain Children
leadingCases.explains: Both sides of the duty must be met. A breach is unlawful, but on its own it is not jurisdictional error.

leadingCases.name: Thompson v Minogue
leadingCases.explains: Once a right is limited, it is for the state to show the limit is demonstrably justified.

grounds.name: Invalid delegated legislation
grounds.plainName: The rule they used may not be valid
grounds.oneLine: The decision rests on a rule the Act may not allow.
grounds.whatItMeans: Parliament passes Acts. It also lets others make rules under those Acts. These rules are called regulations, determinations or by-laws. A rule like that has to stay inside the Act. A rule outside the Act can be invalid.
grounds.plainExample: You get a fine under a council by-law. The by-law bans something the Act never let it ban.
whatRelates: The rule covers something the Act never gave power over.
The rule goes further than the Act allows.
The rule clashes with the Act it was made under, or with another Act.
The rule was made for a purpose the Act was not about.
The rule goes so far that the Act cannot have meant to allow it.
The letter relies on a regulation or a by-law, not an Act.
The rule you were quoted is not in the law the letter names.
You were told the rule and the law say different things.
You were told a rule required this, and nobody could explain why.
Nobody could tell you what the rule was made for.
grounds.whatItIsNot: It does not mean regulations and by-laws are not real law. Most of them are valid. Courts set a high bar before setting one aside. Showing a rule is invalid is also only the first step. You then have to show what that meant for your own decision.
grounds.test: A rule made under an Act has to stay within that Act. The court asks whether the rule can reasonably be seen as appropriate and adapted to the purpose the Act set. That leaves real room for the rule-maker.

elements.name: Inside the subject the Act allows
elements.layPrompt: Does the letter name both a rule and the Act behind it?

elements.name: Not inconsistent with the Act
elements.layPrompt: Were you told the rule and the Act say different things?

elements.name: Made for the Act's purpose
elements.layPrompt: Could anyone tell you what the rule was made for?

elements.name: Appropriate and adapted
elements.layPrompt: Were you told why such a strict rule applied to you?

leadingCases.name: R v Toohey; Ex parte Northern Land Council (1981) 151 CLR 170
leadingCases.explains: A rule made for a purpose outside the Act is not valid, even if it looks valid.

leadingCases.name: Vanstone v Clark (2005) 147 FCR 299
leadingCases.explains: Such a rule has to be appropriate and adapted to the Act's purpose.

leadingCases.name: Project Blue Sky Inc v Australian Broadcasting Authority (1998) 194 CLR 355
leadingCases.explains: Whether a breach makes an act invalid depends on what the Act intended.

grounds.name: Error of law
grounds.plainName: They got the law wrong
grounds.oneLine: The decision-maker applied the wrong legal test, or misread what the law requires.
grounds.whatItMeans: A decision can be challenged where the decision-maker made a legal error — for example, applying the wrong test, misreading what a law requires, or misunderstanding a legal word. Some legal errors are reviewable even when they appear on the face of the written decision.
grounds.plainExample: A decision applies a stricter test than the law actually sets.
whatRelates: The decision seems to apply the wrong rule or test.
The written reasons misstate what the law requires.
A legal word or requirement looks like it was misunderstood.
grounds.whatItIsNot: It does not cover a disagreement about the facts — it is about the law being applied wrongly.
grounds.test: An error of law happens where the decision-maker had the power but got the law wrong. That can mean misreading a word in the Act, using the wrong test, or misunderstanding the limits of the power. Some of these errors go to the power itself. Others show on the face of the reasons and may still be corrected.

elements.name: Wrong legal test
elements.layPrompt: Did they use the wrong legal test or standard?

elements.name: Misreading the law
elements.layPrompt: Do the reasons misstate what the law requires?

leadingCases.name: Craig v South Australia (1995) 184 CLR 163
leadingCases.explains: Distinguishes errors of law within power from errors that take a decision-maker outside it.

leadingCases.name: Kirk v Industrial Court (NSW) (2010) 239 CLR 531
leadingCases.explains: An error that shows on the face of the record can be corrected, even where it did not go to the power itself.

leadingCases.name: Collector of Customs v Agfa-Gevaert Ltd (1996) 186 CLR 389
leadingCases.explains: Where the line runs between a question of fact and a question of law.

grounds.name: Illogical or irrational reasoning
grounds.plainName: The reasons do not follow
grounds.oneLine: A conclusion has to follow from what the decision-maker had.
grounds.whatItMeans: A decision can be wrong in the way it reasons. Not merely arguable, but with no sensible path from the material to the answer. This is close to unreasonableness. It looks at the steps rather than the outcome.
grounds.plainExample: The letter accepts your doctor's report. It then says you have no health problem.
whatRelates: Two things the letter says cannot both be true.
The letter accepts something and then decides the opposite.
A conclusion appears with no step in between.
The reasons rely on something the letter itself rules out.
grounds.whatItIsNot: This is not about the decision being harsh, or about you disagreeing. It is about reasoning that does not hold together. Not every slip in logic counts. Where reasonable people could draw different conclusions from the same evidence, preferring one of them is not illogical.
grounds.test: A conclusion reached with no logical or rational path from the material is not a proper exercise of the power. The threshold is whether no rational decision-maker could have reached that conclusion on that evidence.

elements.name: A step that does not follow
elements.layPrompt: Do two parts of the letter contradict each other?

elements.name: A missing step
elements.layPrompt: Does the letter jump to a conclusion with nothing in between?

leadingCases.name: Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v SZMDS (2010) 240 CLR 611
leadingCases.explains: Reasoning with no logical path to its conclusion can make a decision invalid.

leadingCases.name: Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v Li (2013) 249 CLR 332
leadingCases.explains: A decision needs a reason you can see and follow.

grounds.name: Improper purpose
grounds.plainName: The power was used for the wrong reason
grounds.oneLine: A power was used to get something it was not given for.
grounds.whatItMeans: Parliament gives each power for a reason. The power has to be used for that reason. Using it to get something else can be unlawful. This holds even if the decision-maker meant well.
grounds.plainExample: A housing officer refuses your transfer request. The real reason is a complaint you made about something else.
whatRelates: The reason you were given does not match what the rules are for.
The decision followed soon after you made a complaint.
You were told the decision would send a message to others.
The reason you were given changed when you asked about it.
The decision seems aimed at something the rules never mention.
grounds.whatItIsNot: It does not mean the decision-maker is a bad person. A well-meant decision can still use a power the wrong way. Courts do not assume this lightly.
grounds.test: A statutory power may only be used for the purpose it was given for. If another purpose was a substantial reason, the use may be unlawful. It is for the person challenging the decision to show that, and it is not assumed.

elements.name: The purpose the power was given for
elements.layPrompt: Do the rules say what this power is meant to do?

elements.name: A different purpose at work
elements.layPrompt: Does the real reason look like something else?

elements.name: That other purpose was substantial
elements.layPrompt: Did that other reason come up when the decision was explained?

leadingCases.name: R v Toohey; Ex parte Northern Land Council (1981) 151 CLR 170
leadingCases.explains: A power used for a purpose the Act never gave it is not a valid use.

leadingCases.name: Schlieske v Minister for Immigration and Ethnic Affairs (1988) 84 ALR 719
leadingCases.explains: A wide power still has to be used for the purposes of the Act.

leadingCases.name: Samrein Pty Ltd v Metropolitan Water Sewerage and Drainage Board (1982) 41 ALR 467
leadingCases.explains: The improper purpose need not be the only purpose, only a substantial one.

grounds.name: Inflexible application of policy / acting under dictation
grounds.plainName: They followed a rule or an order instead of deciding your case
grounds.oneLine: A rule can be applied so rigidly that a person is never considered.
grounds.whatItMeans: A decision-maker who has a discretion must actually use it. Applying a policy with no room for your circumstances can be unlawful. So can simply doing what another person told them to do.
grounds.plainExample: You ask for more time to pay a fine. You are told 'we never do that', with no questions asked.
whatRelates: You were told 'that is just our policy', and nothing more.
Nobody asked about your circumstances before saying no.
The decision-maker seemed to be following someone else's instruction.
Your written reasons repeat a general rule and stop there.
You had something new to say, and nobody would hear it.
grounds.whatItIsNot: It does not mean policies are banned. It means a policy cannot leave your own case unheard.
grounds.test: A decision-maker with a choice must really make it. A policy cannot be applied as a fixed rule. They also cannot just do what someone else says.

elements.name: Inflexible application of policy
elements.layPrompt: Was a general rule applied without looking at your situation?

elements.name: Acting under dictation
elements.layPrompt: Did the decision-maker simply do what someone else told them?

leadingCases.name: Re Drake (No 2)
leadingCases.explains: A policy may guide a decision. It may not replace it.

leadingCases.name: Green v Daniels (1977) 13 ALR 1
leadingCases.explains: A rule was applied so rigidly that the person was never considered.

grounds.name: Invalid delegation
grounds.plainName: The wrong person made the decision
grounds.oneLine: The law named one person to decide, and someone else decided.
grounds.whatItMeans: An Act names who holds a power. Often that person can act through their staff. Sometimes the Act means they have to decide it themselves. If someone else decides, the decision can be unlawful.
grounds.plainExample: Your payment is cancelled by a team leader. The Act gives that decision to the Secretary.
whatRelates: The power is one the Act gave to a named person by name.
The department is large, and the power is used very often.
The letter is signed by someone with a different job title.
The letter names no person at all, only a team.
The rules name one office, but a different office wrote to you.
You were told a senior officer decided, but someone else signed.
Nothing in the letter shows the signer was allowed to decide.
grounds.whatItIsNot: It does not mean staff can never act for a minister. Many powers are used that way every day. The question is what the Act requires.
grounds.test: Whether a subordinate may use the power depends on the Act. The court asks if the Act requires the named person to decide personally.

elements.name: Who the Act names
elements.layPrompt: Which office does the letter say the decision belongs to?

elements.name: Whether that person had to decide it
elements.layPrompt: Does the letter say the named person decided it themselves?

elements.name: Whether the signer was authorised
elements.layPrompt: Does anything show the signer was allowed to decide?

leadingCases.name: Minister for Aboriginal Affairs v Peko-Wallsend Ltd (1986) 162 CLR 24
leadingCases.explains: A minister can often act through staff. That is not true of every power.

leadingCases.name: Pattenden v Commissioner of Taxation [2008] FCA 1590
leadingCases.explains: Whether a subordinate may sign in the named person's place depends on the Act.

grounds.name: Irrelevant considerations
grounds.plainName: They relied on something that should not have mattered
grounds.oneLine: The law can also name things a decision-maker must leave out.
grounds.whatItMeans: Some Acts say what a decision-maker may not take into account. Relying on a forbidden matter can make a decision unlawful. This point often travels with a claim about the wrong purpose.
grounds.plainExample: A fine is upheld partly because you complained about the officer. Your complaint had nothing to do with the fine.
whatRelates: The reasons mention something that has nothing to do with the rules.
Your past, your attitude, or an old complaint seems to have counted.
A staff member raised a topic the rules never mention.
The outcome seems driven by something outside the scheme.
Cost or convenience seems to have driven a decision about your needs.
grounds.whatItIsNot: It does not cover every fact you think was unfair. The law must actually put that matter out of bounds.
grounds.test: An Act may forbid certain matters from being taken into account. Relying on a forbidden matter can make the decision invalid.

elements.name: A matter the law puts out of bounds
elements.layPrompt: Do the rules say this topic should not affect the decision?

elements.name: The decision-maker relied on it
elements.layPrompt: Does that topic appear in the reasons you were given?

leadingCases.name: Minister for Aboriginal Affairs v Peko-Wallsend Ltd (1986) 162 CLR 24
leadingCases.explains: The same Act can also imply which matters must be left out.

grounds.name: Jurisdictional error
grounds.plainName: The decision-maker went beyond their power
grounds.oneLine: The decision-maker acted outside their power, or asked the wrong question.
grounds.whatItMeans: A decision can be unlawful if the decision-maker acted beyond the power the law gives them — for example by asking the wrong question, ignoring a step the law required first, or misunderstanding the limits of their role. This is a central idea in judicial review, especially for Commonwealth decisions.
grounds.plainExample: A body decides something only a different body had the power to decide.
whatRelates: The decision-maker may not have had the power to make this decision.
A step the law required first seems to have been skipped.
The decision-maker seems to have misunderstood what they were allowed to decide.
grounds.whatItIsNot: It does not mean any mistake — it has to be an error that goes to the decision-maker's power.
grounds.test: An error going to the existence or exercise of power (a jurisdictional error) may make a decision invalid.

elements.name: Acting beyond power
elements.layPrompt: Did the decision-maker act outside what the law lets them do?

elements.name: Asking the wrong question
elements.layPrompt: Did they decide on the wrong question, or ignore a required step?

leadingCases.name: Craig v South Australia (1995) 184 CLR 163
leadingCases.explains: Sets out the classic errors. Asking the wrong question. Ignoring material it had to consider. Misunderstanding the power it was given.

leadingCases.name: Kirk v Industrial Court (NSW) (2010) 239 CLR 531
leadingCases.explains: A State Supreme Court can always check for this kind of error. Parliament cannot take that away.

leadingCases.name: Plaintiff S157/2002 v Commonwealth (2003) 211 CLR 476
leadingCases.explains: A law can say a decision is final. That still does not protect a decision made outside the power.

grounds.name: No evidence / mistake of material fact
grounds.plainName: A key finding had no evidence behind it
grounds.oneLine: A finding that mattered was made with no evidence to support it.
grounds.whatItMeans: A decision can be challenged if a finding on a key fact was made with no evidence at all to support it, or rested on a clear mistake about a fact the decision turned on. It is not enough that the evidence was weak — there must be no evidence, or a clear error on a central point.
grounds.plainExample: A debt is raised on the basis you were paid on dates that the records show you were not.
whatRelates: A key finding was made with nothing to support it.
The decision turned on a fact that is simply wrong.
Evidence you gave that contradicts a central finding appears to have been overlooked.
grounds.whatItIsNot: It does not cover a decision you just think got the facts wrong on balance — the error has to be on a critical point with no support.
grounds.test: A material finding made with no evidence, or a decision based on a mistake of a material fact, may be reviewable.

elements.name: No evidence for a key finding
elements.layPrompt: Was there an important finding with no evidence at all behind it?

elements.name: Mistake about a central fact
elements.layPrompt: Did the decision rely on a fact that is plainly wrong?

leadingCases.name: Australian Broadcasting Tribunal v Bond (1990) 170 CLR 321
leadingCases.explains: Findings have to rest on evidence that actually proves something, not on nothing.

leadingCases.name: Corporation of the City of Enfield v Development Assessment Commission (2000) 199 CLR 135
leadingCases.explains: Some facts must actually exist before a power can be used — and a court can check for itself.

grounds.name: A fact the power depended on
grounds.plainName: A fact the law required was not there
grounds.oneLine: Some powers only exist if a certain fact is true.
grounds.whatItMeans: Sometimes an Act says a decision can only be made if a particular thing is true. That thing has to really be true. It is not enough that the decision-maker believed it. A court can look at that fact for itself.
grounds.plainExample: A rule lets an office act only if you live in a certain area. You do not live there. They acted anyway.
whatRelates: The letter relies on a fact about you that is simply not true.
You can show the opposite with a document you already hold.
The rule you were given applies to a group you are not part of.
The letter says you were somewhere, or held something, that you did not.
grounds.whatItIsNot: This is not about a judgement call, like whether something was reasonable. It is about a plain fact that is either true or not.
grounds.test: Where a power depends on a fact existing, that fact must exist. A court can decide it for itself.

elements.name: The fact the power needed
elements.layPrompt: Does the letter rely on a fact about you that is not true?

elements.name: Something that shows it
elements.layPrompt: Do you have a document or record that shows the real position?

leadingCases.name: Plaintiff M70/2011 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (2011) 244 CLR 144
leadingCases.explains: A power that depends on a country meeting set conditions needs those conditions to be really met.

leadingCases.name: City of Enfield v Development Assessment Commission (2000) 199 CLR 135
leadingCases.explains: A court can decide such a fact for itself, not just review the view taken.

grounds.name: Procedural fairness — the rule against bias
grounds.plainName: The person deciding was not neutral
grounds.oneLine: The person deciding must not have a stake, or a closed mind.
grounds.whatItMeans: The person deciding must come to your case with an open mind. They should not have money or personal ties to the result. There are two separate versions of this. One asks what was actually in their mind. The other asks how the situation would look to a fair-minded onlooker. The second one is the more usual way it is raised.
grounds.plainExample: The council officer who looked into your case also decided your fine. Nobody else took part.
whatRelates: The same person looked into your case and then decided it.
The decision-maker had already said what they thought.
The decision-maker had money or family ties to the result.
You were told the answer before you finished explaining.
The decision-maker had a role at an earlier stage.
grounds.whatItIsNot: It does not mean the decision-maker must have no views. A firm view is not the same as a closed mind. Showing what was really in someone's mind is a high bar, so the fair-minded-onlooker version is the one usually relied on.
grounds.test: For a reasonable apprehension of bias, a decision-maker is disqualified if a fair-minded lay observer might reasonably apprehend that they might not bring an impartial mind to the question. The question is one of possibility, real and not remote, rather than probability. For actual bias, the state of mind must be so committed to a conclusion already formed as to be incapable of alteration.

elements.name: Something that might sway the decision-maker
elements.layPrompt: Did they have an interest, an earlier role, or a stated view?

elements.name: A link between that thing and this decision
elements.layPrompt: Can you join the dots between that thing and the decision going the way it did?

elements.name: A mind already made up
elements.layPrompt: Did they seem unable to change their mind, whatever you said?

leadingCases.name: Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs v Jia Legeng (2001) 205 CLR 507
leadingCases.explains: Actual bias means a mind so fixed it cannot be changed. Having leanings one way is not enough.

leadingCases.name: Ebner v Official Trustee in Bankruptcy (2000) 205 CLR 337
leadingCases.pinpoint: Gleeson CJ, McHugh, Gummow and Hayne JJ
leadingCases.explains: The other version asks what a fair-minded onlooker might think. It has two steps. First, name the thing that might pull the decision off course. Then show how it connects to this decision.

grounds.name: Procedural fairness — the hearing rule
grounds.plainName: You never got to have your say
grounds.oneLine: You usually get told what is coming, and a real chance to reply.
grounds.whatItMeans: A decision-maker usually has to tell you what is being decided. You usually get a real chance to reply before it happens. If something important counts against you, and it is the sort of thing a decision-maker would rely on, you usually get to see it first.
grounds.plainExample: Centrelink raises a debt using a report you were never shown. Nobody asked you to explain.
whatRelates: You did not know a decision about you was coming.
Nobody asked you to explain your side of it.
Something was used against you that you never saw.
You asked to speak to someone, and were told no.
The process changed part way, and nobody told you.
They decided it on a different basis than you were led to expect, and you never got to answer that.
grounds.whatItIsNot: This is about the process, not the result. It does not mean the answer would have been different. There is also no single picture of what a fair hearing looks like. Depending on the power and the situation it can mean a full hearing, or very little.
grounds.test: First, does a fair hearing duty apply to this power? Second, what did that duty require in that situation? Both come from the Act and the facts.

elements.name: The duty applies
elements.layPrompt: Could this decision affect your rights, your money, or your home?

elements.name: Notice of what was being decided
elements.layPrompt: Were you told what was being looked at before it was decided?

elements.name: Information against you was shown to you
elements.layPrompt: Was something used against you that you never got to see?

elements.name: A real chance to respond
elements.layPrompt: Did you get a real chance to reply before the decision?

leadingCases.name: Badari v Minister for Territory Families and Urban Housing [2025] HCA 47
leadingCases.pinpoint: Gageler CJ, Gordon, Edelman, Steward and Gleeson JJ
leadingCases.explains: A power to change a person's rent is presumed to require fairness.

leadingCases.name: Saeed v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (2010) 241 CLR 252
leadingCases.explains: Whether the duty applies is worked out by reading the Act.

leadingCases.name: Kioa v West (1985) 159 CLR 550
leadingCases.explains: Key information counting against a person should usually be shown to them.

leadingCases.name: Minister for Immigration and Border Protection v WZARH (2015) 256 CLR 326
leadingCases.explains: Changing the promised process without telling the person can be unfair.

leadingCases.name: Nathanson v Minister for Home Affairs (2022) 276 CLR 80
leadingCases.pinpoint: Kiefel CJ, Keane and Gleeson JJ
leadingCases.explains: Deciding on a new issue without notice can deny a fair hearing.

grounds.name: Relevant considerations
grounds.plainName: They ignored something they had to take into account
grounds.oneLine: The law can name things a decision-maker must take into account.
grounds.whatItMeans: Some Acts say what a decision-maker must take into account. Missing one of those matters can make a decision unlawful. In Victoria, public bodies must also think about your human rights.
grounds.plainExample: You send Centrelink medical reports about your illness. The debt decision never mentions them.
whatRelates: You gave them information that the decision never mentions.
Something the rules say must be weighed appears to have been left out.
Your reasons letter skips a matter you raised in writing.
A report or assessment you sent in is not discussed anywhere.
You are in Victoria and a human right may be affected.
grounds.whatItIsNot: It does not mean every point you raised had to be accepted. The required matters only had to be genuinely considered.
grounds.test: An Act may require certain matters to be taken into account. It can say so outright, or it can be implied from what the Act is for. Failing to consider a required matter can make the decision invalid.

elements.name: A matter the law required them to consider
elements.layPrompt: Do the rules list something they had to take into account?

elements.name: That matter was not considered
elements.layPrompt: Does the decision look like it left that matter out?

elements.name: Proper consideration of a human right (Victoria)
elements.layPrompt: Are you in Victoria? Did this affect your home, family or privacy?

leadingCases.name: Certain Children v Minister for Families and Children (No 2) (2017) 52 VR 441
leadingCases.explains: In Victoria, Charter rights can be part of what a decision-maker must weigh.

leadingCases.name: Minister for Aboriginal Affairs v Peko-Wallsend Ltd (1986) 162 CLR 24
leadingCases.explains: The Act decides which matters a decision-maker must take into account.

leadingCases.name: Tickner v Chapman (1995) 57 FCR 451
leadingCases.explains: A matter the law lists must be really thought about, not just filed.

leadingCases.name: Bare v Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (2015) 48 VR 129
leadingCases.explains: In Victoria, a public body must think about your human rights too.

leadingCases.name: Thompson v Minogue (2021) 67 VR 301
leadingCases.explains: A Victorian court applied that human rights duty to prison conditions.

grounds.name: A state of mind the power depended on
grounds.plainName: They had to be satisfied of something first
grounds.oneLine: Some powers only exist once the decision-maker is satisfied of something.
grounds.whatItMeans: Sometimes an Act says a decision can be made if the decision-maker is satisfied of something. Courts describe this in two ways. One looks at whether the reasoning holds together. The other asks whether the conclusion was open to them on the material they had. The bar is a high one either way.
grounds.plainExample: A rule lets an office act if it is satisfied you were told. Nobody looked at whether you were told.
whatRelates: The letter states a conclusion about you with nothing behind it.
The reasons skip straight to the answer.
The material in front of them pointed the other way.
Two parts of the letter cannot both be true.
grounds.whatItIsNot: This is not about disagreeing with the outcome. It is about whether they really formed the view the law asked them to form. Not every slip in logic counts, and a court will be slow to step in.
grounds.test: Where a power depends on the decision-maker being satisfied of something, that state of satisfaction must be reached on a rational basis. The threshold is whether no rational decision-maker could have reached that conclusion on that evidence.

elements.name: The thing they had to be satisfied of
elements.layPrompt: Does the letter say they were satisfied of something about you?

elements.name: A path to that view
elements.layPrompt: Do the reasons show how they got to that view?

leadingCases.name: Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v SZMDS (2010) 240 CLR 611
leadingCases.explains: A view held with no logical path to it is not the state of mind the law asked for.

leadingCases.name: Plaintiff M70/2011 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (2011) 244 CLR 144
leadingCases.explains: Where a power depends on the decision-maker forming a state of mind, that state of mind is itself the thing the power depends on.

grounds.name: Unlawful policy
grounds.plainName: The policy itself does not match the law
grounds.oneLine: A policy cannot cut down what the Act allows.
grounds.whatItMeans: Departments write policies to guide their staff. A policy must fit inside the Act it sits under. A policy cannot contradict the Act. It also cannot remove a choice the Act gives.
grounds.plainExample: An Act lets Centrelink waive a debt in special cases. A policy tells staff to never waive a debt.
whatRelates: You were quoted a policy rule that the Act does not contain.
The policy turns a 'may' in the Act into a 'never'.
A guideline seems to add a condition the law never set.
Staff say they have no choice, but the Act gives one.
The policy and the wording of the law seem to disagree.
grounds.whatItIsNot: Policies are allowed, and they are useful. The question is whether this policy fits the Act.
grounds.test: A policy must be consistent with the Act it operates under. A policy that removes a discretion the Act gives may be unlawful.

elements.name: A policy or guideline was used
elements.layPrompt: Were you told a policy or guideline decided the outcome?

elements.name: The policy conflicts with the Act
elements.layPrompt: Does the policy seem to say something different from the law?

elements.name: The policy removes a choice the Act gives
elements.layPrompt: Does the Act say 'may', where the policy says 'never'?

leadingCases.name: Re Drake (No 2)
leadingCases.explains: A policy must leave the decision-maker's discretion intact.

leadingCases.name: Green v Daniels (1977) 13 ALR 1
leadingCases.explains: A policy cannot override what the Act says.

grounds.name: Legal unreasonableness
grounds.plainName: The decision was one no reasonable decision-maker could make
grounds.oneLine: Even with power, a decision can be unlawful if it lacks any sensible justification.
grounds.whatItMeans: Even where a decision-maker has the power, the decision can be unlawful if it lacks an evident and intelligible justification on the material before them, or is so unreasonable that no reasonable decision-maker could have reached it. This is a high bar — it is not enough to disagree.
grounds.plainExample: A penalty far out of proportion to a tiny, first-time mistake, with no explanation.
whatRelates: The outcome seems to make no sense on the facts the decision-maker had.
The result is far harsher than the situation called for.
There is no intelligible reason given for the decision.
grounds.whatItIsNot: It does not mean you simply disagree with the decision — it has to lack a sensible basis.
grounds.test: A decision may be unlawful if it lacks an evident and intelligible justification, or is one no reasonable decision-maker could have reached.

elements.name: No intelligible justification
elements.layPrompt: Does the outcome seem to make no sense on the facts the decision-maker had?

elements.name: Disproportionate or arbitrary
elements.layPrompt: Was the result far harsher than the situation called for, or seemingly arbitrary?

leadingCases.name: Minister for Home Affairs v DUA16 (2020) 271 CLR 550
leadingCases.explains: Heard with a second case that went the other way. Whether a failure is unreasonable turns on the statute and on what actually went wrong.

leadingCases.name: Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223
leadingCases.explains: Where this ground began. A decision can be so unreasonable that no reasonable body could have made it.

leadingCases.name: Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v Li (2013) 249 CLR 332
leadingCases.explains: The test used in Australia now. A decision needs a reason you can see and follow.

leadingCases.name: Minister for Immigration and Border Protection v SZVFW (2018) 264 CLR 541
leadingCases.explains: The test is a stringent one. A court will not step in lightly where the law leaves the choice to the decision-maker.

grounds.name: Acting without legal authority
grounds.plainName: They never had the power to do this
grounds.oneLine: Some decisions are made without the power the law requires.
grounds.whatItMeans: Every government power comes from an Act of Parliament. The Act sets the limits of that power. A decision outside those limits has no legal authority behind it. The letter should tell you which law it relies on.
grounds.plainExample: A letter raises a debt against you. The Act gives that office no power to raise debts.
whatRelates: The letter does not name the law it was made under.
The letter comes from an office you have never dealt with.
The decision covers something the rules you were given do not mention.
You cannot find the power the letter says it is using.
The letter decides something you thought only a court could decide.
grounds.whatItIsNot: This is not about whether the decision was harsh or unfair. It asks a narrower question. Did the power exist at all?
grounds.test: A power may only be used within the limits the Act sets. Acting outside those limits is acting without legal authority.

elements.name: A law that gives the power
elements.layPrompt: Does the letter name the law it was made under?

elements.name: Staying inside the limits
elements.layPrompt: Is the decision about something the rules you were given never mention?

elements.name: The office the law names
elements.layPrompt: Does the office named in the letter match the one that wrote to you?

leadingCases.name: ABC Developmental Learning Centres Pty Ltd v Secretary, Department of Human Services [2007] VSC 37
leadingCases.explains: Acting outside the scope the Act allows is acting without authority.

leadingCases.name: Hossain v Minister for Immigration and Border Protection (2018) 264 CLR 123
leadingCases.explains: An Act sets the limits of the power it gives out.

leadingCases.name: Craig v South Australia (1995) 184 CLR 163
leadingCases.explains: One classic error is acting beyond the power the law gives.

leadingCases.name: Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs v Bhardwaj (2002) 209 CLR 597
leadingCases.explains: A decision made outside the power counts in law as no decision.

leadingCases.name: Attorney-General (NSW) v Quin (1990) 170 CLR 1
leadingCases.explains: A court checks whether a decision was lawful, not whether it was right.

concepts.name: Justiciability
concepts.plainName: Some decisions a court will not look at
concepts.oneLine: A few kinds of government action sit outside what a court will review.
concepts.whatItMeans: Courts review government decisions. But not every act of government is the kind of thing a court will rule on. Some choices belong to the elected government, not to a judge. What matters is the subject matter, not where the power came from. Everyday decisions made under an Act are the ordinary case, and courts do review those.
concepts.whatItIsNot: This is not a hurdle for ordinary decisions. A Centrelink debt, a fine, a housing refusal or a licence decision is made under an Act, and that is exactly the kind of decision courts review every day. This narrow rule is about things like going to war.
keyPoints: Decisions made under an Act are the normal case, and they are reviewable.
A small group of powers sits further from review — things like foreign relations, national security, or a decision to go to war.
What counts is the subject matter of the power, not the label on where it came from.
Courts are more willing to step in where the action directly affects one person's rights or interests.
They are less willing where the action is political in nature and affects the public at large.

leadingCases.name: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service
leadingCases.explains: What decides this is the subject matter of the power, not the source it came from.

leadingCases.name: Minister for Arts Heritage and the Environment v Peko-Wallsend Ltd (1987) 15 FCR 274
leadingCases.explains: These powers were once beyond review altogether. That is no longer so.

sources: Owner's administrative-law knowledge base (Review Notes; JR Hypo, 2026-08-19)

concepts.name: The two ways into a federal court
concepts.plainName: There is more than one door
concepts.oneLine: Commonwealth decisions can be challenged by two different routes.
concepts.whatItMeans: For an Australian Government decision there is more than one way to ask a court to check it. One is a statute made for the job. It is the more straightforward route. The other is the court's older, wider power. Each reaches slightly different things. Which one fits is a question for a lawyer, not something you have to work out.
concepts.whatItIsNot: This is not a choice you need to make before you get help. You do not have to name a route to ask a free legal service for advice. It is here so the question makes sense when someone asks it.
keyPoints: There is more than one way to bring a Commonwealth decision to a court.
The statutory route is described as the more straightforward one.
It covers a decision of an administrative character made under an Act. It also covers some conduct leading up to a decision, and a failure to decide when there was a duty to.
Some decisions are carved out of it, including decisions of the Governor-General.
The wider route reaches things the statutory one does not, such as powers that do not come from an Act, and the validity of rules and regulations.

options.name: The Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 (Cth)
options.whatItDoes: Lets a federal court review a decision of an administrative character made under an Act. It is the more straightforward and less technical route.
options.note: It does not reach every Commonwealth decision. Some are excluded by the Act itself.

options.name: Section 39B of the Judiciary Act 1903 (Cth)
options.whatItDoes: A broader power. It reaches powers that do not come from an Act, and the validity of rules and regulations.
options.note: It is not limited in the same way as the statutory route, but it is more technical.

leadingCases.name: Griffith University v Tang (2005) 221 CLR 99
leadingCases.explains: The decision must be one an Act required or allowed. It must also affect legal rights or duties, and get that power from the Act itself.

leadingCases.name: Australian Broadcasting Tribunal v Bond
leadingCases.explains: The decision is usually one that settles something, rather than a step along the way.

concepts.name: What a court can give you
concepts.plainName: What you can actually walk away with
concepts.oneLine: A court can undo a decision. It cannot make a new one for you.
concepts.whatItMeans: This is the part people are most often surprised by. If a court finds the decision was not made lawfully, it can wipe it out. It can order the decision-maker to do their job. It can stop them acting unlawfully. What it cannot do is decide the matter itself. The file goes back, and the same body decides it again, this time properly.
concepts.whatItIsNot: It is not a way to get the answer you wanted. A court will not grant your payment, cancel your debt, or give you the licence. If that is what you need, a tribunal is the path that can do it, where a law allows one.
keyPoints: A court can set a decision aside and send it back.
It cannot substitute its own decision for the decision-maker's.
The same body usually decides again. It may reach the same answer, lawfully this time.
Which remedy you ask for shapes which court you go to, and who is allowed to ask.
Remedies are discretionary, though a court starts from the position of granting relief where a case is made out.

options.name: Certiorari
options.whatItDoes: Cancels the legal effect of a decision that was not made lawfully.
options.note: In the High Court this is asked for alongside one of the orders below, rather than on its own.

options.name: Mandamus
options.whatItDoes: Orders a public official to carry out a duty they owe, according to law.
options.note: It works where a duty has been left undone. It does not work where the law leaves the choice to them.

options.name: Prohibition
options.whatItDoes: Stops a decision-maker from deciding unlawfully, or from carrying on an unlawful course of action.
options.note: Useful while something is still happening, rather than after it is over.

options.name: Injunction
options.plainName: An order to do or stop something
options.whatItDoes: Orders someone to do a particular thing, or to stop doing one.
options.note: You need a legal right of your own for this one.

options.name: Declaration
options.plainName: A statement of where you stand
options.whatItDoes: A formal statement of what the legal position is, without ordering anyone to do anything.
options.note: There has to be a real dispute. A court will not answer a hypothetical question.

leadingCases.name: Ainsworth v Criminal Justice Commission
leadingCases.explains: Wiping out a decision is about its legal effect. A declaration states where the parties stand.

leadingCases.name: City of Enfield v Development Assessment Commission (2000) 199 CLR 135
leadingCases.explains: A court has a choice about granting relief, but it starts from the position of granting it.

sources: Owner's administrative-law knowledge base (JR Hypo; Combined MR/JR Framework, 2026-08-19)

concepts.name: Standing
concepts.plainName: Whether you are the right person to bring it
concepts.oneLine: If the decision was about you, this is almost never the problem.
concepts.whatItMeans: Before anyone looks at your case, there is a question of whether you are the right person to raise it. This is called standing. If the decision was made about you, and it affects your money, your home, your payment or your licence, you will normally have it. The question really matters for people further from the decision, such as a group objecting on behalf of others.
concepts.whatItIsNot: It is not a test of how strong your case is. It only asks whether you are the right person to bring it. Someone can have standing and still not succeed, and someone can care deeply and still not have standing.
keyPoints: If the decision was about you and affects you, standing is rarely the obstacle.
The test is not the same for every route.
At a tribunal, the law for your decision usually says who may apply. It is often anyone whose interests are affected.
Interests are read broadly. They are not limited to money or property, and they can be affected indirectly.
For a court, a general concern about government is not enough on its own.

options.name: Merits review at a tribunal
options.whatItDoes: The law that created the review right usually says who may apply. Often that is a person whose interests are affected by the decision.
options.note: Interests are read widely. They are not limited to money or property, and it does not matter that someone else is affected too.

options.name: The statutory route to a federal court
options.whatItDoes: Asks whether you are a person aggrieved. This is not read narrowly.
options.note: It means something beyond what any member of the public has. Harm to your economic interests can be enough.

options.name: Asking a court to wipe out or stop a decision
options.whatItDoes: Asks whether the decision has a sufficient effect on your legal rights or interests.
options.note: Damage to a personal or business reputation can count.

options.name: Asking a court to make someone do their duty
options.whatItDoes: Asks whether you have a sufficient interest, or a special legal right, in seeing a public duty carried out.
options.note: The starting question is whether a duty is genuinely left undone.

options.name: Asking for an order or a statement of your position
options.whatItDoes: Asks for a special interest in the subject matter — more than an ordinary member of the public has.
options.note: A purely emotional or intellectual concern is not enough on its own. An order to do or stop something needs a legal right.

leadingCases.name: Australian Conservation Foundation v Commonwealth
leadingCases.explains: A special interest is needed. Caring about an issue, without more, is not enough.

leadingCases.name: Onus v Alcoa
leadingCases.explains: A cultural or religious connection to what is at stake can be a special interest.

leadingCases.name: Argos Pty Ltd v Corbell
leadingCases.explains: Harm to your economic interests can make you a person aggrieved.

sources: Owner's administrative-law knowledge base (JR Hypo; Review Notes, 2026-08-19)

concepts.name: Reasons and freedom of information
concepts.plainName: Getting the reasons, and getting the documents
concepts.oneLine: Two different requests. One asks why. The other asks to see the file.
concepts.whatItMeans: There are two separate things you can ask for, and people often mix them up. You can ask the decision-maker for a written statement of reasons. That tells you why. You can also make a freedom of information request. That asks to see documents. Asking for reasons is usually the more useful first step, and it is free.
concepts.whatItIsNot: A freedom of information request is not a way to have a decision reviewed. Neither is a request for reasons. They get you information, and information is what tells you whether a review is worth it and what to say.
keyPoints: A written statement of reasons tells you what the decision-maker actually relied on.
Asking for reasons is a useful first step on either review path. Whether they must give them depends on the type of decision.
Freedom of information is a separate right. It asks to see documents rather than to be told why.
If a freedom of information request is refused, that refusal can usually be reviewed.
Time limits apply to both. Check the limit for your decision rather than assuming.

options.name: A statement of reasons
options.whatItDoes: In many cases you can ask the decision-maker for written reasons. Whether there is a legal duty to give them depends on the type of decision.
options.note: For an Australian Government decision this right comes from the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 (Cth) s 13. In Victoria it comes from the Administrative Law Act 1978 (Vic) s 8.

options.name: A freedom of information request
options.whatItDoes: Asks an agency for copies of documents it holds, including documents about you.
options.note: The Freedom of Information Act 1982 applies federally, and Victoria has an Act of the same name. Charges may apply. A refusal can usually be reviewed. The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner and the Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner are common review bodies for FOI decisions.

sources: Owner's administrative-law knowledge base (Combined MR/JR Framework; Venture Concepts, 2026-08-19)
Office of the Australian Information Commissioner — oaic.gov.au
Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner — ovic.vic.gov.au

concepts.name: The Ombudsman
concepts.plainName: A free complaint about how you were treated
concepts.oneLine: Complaining is free, but the Ombudsman cannot change your decision.
concepts.whatItMeans: The Ombudsman takes complaints about government departments and agencies. Complaining is free. It can look at how a decision was made, and at how you were treated along the way. What it cannot do is overturn or change the decision. That is the difference between the Ombudsman and a tribunal or a court.
concepts.whatItIsNot: It is not a review body. Many people expect a complaint to reverse a decision, and it cannot. Even where the Ombudsman agrees with you, the decision itself still stands. A complaint also runs separately from any review, so a review time limit keeps running while you wait.
keyPoints: Complaining to the Ombudsman is free.
The Ombudsman cannot overturn or change a decision.
It can look at how a decision was made, and how you were treated.
Where no law gives a right to review, this is one of the paths that remains — a court is the other.
A complaint is separate from a review. Keep track of any review time limit as well.

options.name: Commonwealth Ombudsman
options.whatItDoes: Takes free complaints about Australian Government departments and agencies, including Services Australia.
options.note: There is no strict time limit on complaining, but sooner is usually better. Complaints go through ombudsman.gov.au.

options.name: Victorian Ombudsman
options.whatItDoes: Takes free complaints about Victorian government bodies, including councils and agencies.
options.note: The usual step is to complain to the organisation first. Complaints go through ombudsman.vic.gov.au.

sources: Owner's administrative-law knowledge base (Combined MR/JR Framework, 2026-08-19)

triage.mrVsJr: Merits review asks 'what is the correct or preferable decision?' — a tribunal stands in the decision-maker's shoes and can change the outcome. Judicial review asks 'was the decision lawful?' — a court checks the process and can set a decision aside, but cannot substitute its own. Choose by what the person wants: a different outcome points to merits review (if available); an unlawful process, or no merits-review right, points to judicial review. The avenue, body and time limit for a specific decision come from the lawyer-verified procedural layer, never from here.

remedies.mr: affirm, vary, or set aside and substitute the decision (merits review)
remedies.jr: quash / set aside and send back to be remade; cannot substitute a new decision (judicial review)
